Gochugaru-Yuja Cabbage Slaw

This slaw is the modern Korean table's answer to coleslaw: napa cabbage in a gochugaru dressing brightened with yuja (Korean citron — marmalade's source) instead of vinegar alone.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4–6 as the table's salad

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary — the citrus build. This slaw is the modern Korean table's answer to coleslaw: napa cabbage in a gochugaru dressing brightened with yuja (Korean citron — marmalade's source) instead of vinegar alone. It carries the geotjeori family's (#B04, #F03) fresh-kimchi logic into a rounder, citrus-forward register, and it is the fresh bowl that best matches the grilled fish records (#SF07, #SF09), whose oiliness wants citrus the way the meat records want scallion (#F02).

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The 10-minute salt draw on the cabbage ribbons — the #B07 law, one leaf over: the stems weep, stay crisp, and stop diluting the dressing. Squeeze gently by the handful after.
  • If yuja-cheong is new: it is the citron preserve sold in every Korean market's tea aisle, syrup with suspended rind — a spoon of it is this dressing's entire personality.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    The dressing whisked smooth — gochugaru, yuja, vinegar, soy — into an amber-red slurry that tastes citrus-first, savory-second, with the gochugaru's warmth behind. Checkpoint — a fingertip taste should read like marmalade that went to the grill table: bright, sweet, a warm hum. Sharper or sweeter is a teaspoon of vinegar or yuja away.
  2. 02
    The squeezed cabbage, scallion, and the dressing tossed — spoons this time, gently, the ribbons are sturdy but the toss is short — sesame oil and seeds through. Checkpoint — the eating test: the stem's snap and the citrus dressing's bright-sweet-heat in one bite, with the yuja rind's bitter-edge flick at the finish — the note that separates this slaw from every honey-and-chili imitation. Beside grilled mackerel (#SF07), the fish's fat and the citrus meet exactly as intended. Chef’s Note — yuja (also sold as yuzu in its Japanese career) is doing structural work in the dressing: its aromatic oils sit in the rind, which is why the marmalade with visible rind beats yuzu juice alone in this build — the bitterness of the peel is the counterweight that keeps a sweet dressing from tipping into dessert. No yuja at all: half a lemon's zest-and-juice plus the honey gets three-quarters of the way, and the slaw remains worth building.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Slaw flooded by servingSkipped the drawThe 10-minute salt and squeeze
Dressing tasted flatJuice-only citrusYuja-cheong with rind, or lemon zest plus juice
Too sweet, jammyYuja-heavyA teaspoon more vinegar
Cabbage ribbons crushedHeavy hand at the tossSpoon-toss, thirty seconds

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Best within 2 hours, edible at a day refrigerated (the ribbons hold better than lettuce); undressed salted cabbage keeps half a day.
  • Variations: matchstick apple folded in for sweetness and snap; the same dressing on cucumber ribbons; a pinch of gochugaru more for the tables that want the slaw to carry heat as well as brightness.
